title: Public concern remains materially grounded while country optimism can move ahead of lived economic satisfaction
source_unit: Ipsos What Worries the World, September 2026

denominator.unit: approximately adults surveyed monthly across 30 countries; exact country samples and weighting are not published on the public summary page

survey_scope.value: most important social and political issues, with more than ten years of trend context

monthly_comparability.value: September results are interpreted against prior monthly and long-term country and issue trends

public_concern_route.value: the study connects economic, health, crime, inequality, corruption, immigration, climate, and political concerns in a common public-attention field

observations.method: Ipsos monthly What Worries the World survey conducted in 30 countries among around 20,000 adults, with more than a decade of repeated waves; the public release provides selected country highlights and says full breakdowns are available on request.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not provide full questionnaires, country-level denominators, weighting details, or all issue results; cross-country percentages should not be treated as a single globally representative population estimate.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 30 countries, with country-specific issue and direction-of-travel differences.
observations.counterinterpretation: Monthly concern shifts may reflect salience, news cycles, seasonality, or sampling variation rather than durable changes in material conditions or political behavior.

denominator.unit: U.S. country result within Ipsos What Worries the World September 2026 wave

healthcare_worry.unit: percent of Americans worried about healthcare

interpretive_route.value: healthcare concern appears as a country-specific public priority within the broader cost, health, and institutional-trust field

observations.method: Ipsos country-level highlight from the September monthly survey; the public page does not publish the U.S. subgroup sample or question wording in full.
observations.uncertainty: A single monthly percentage-point movement may reflect event salience or sampling variation and does not establish changes in healthcare access, affordability, or outcomes.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults in the September 2026 Ipsos wave.
observations.counterinterpretation: Healthcare worry can rise even when access or coverage improves if expectations, political conflict, prices, or media attention change faster than lived conditions.

denominator.unit: Argentina country result within Ipsos What Worries the World September 2026 wave

unemployment_worry.unit: percent in Argentina worried about unemployment

labor_security_route.value: employment concern can act as a bridge between macro conditions, household room, political expectations, and social stability

observations.method: Ipsos country-level highlight from the September monthly survey; full country sample and trend breakdown are not shown on the public summary page.
observations.uncertainty: Worry is not unemployment incidence, job loss, labor-force participation, or income change; the monthly increase does not identify its cause.
observations.subgroup: Adults in Argentina participating in the September 2026 opinion wave.
observations.counterinterpretation: High unemployment concern can coexist with employment gains if job quality, wages, informality, or future expectations remain weak.

observations.period: September 2026; Colombia direction-of-travel and lived-economy gap

denominator.unit: Colombia country result within Ipsos What Worries the World September 2026 wave

right_direction.unit: percent in Colombia saying the country is heading in the right direction

annual_change.unit: percentage-point increase from a year earlier; 38% global comparison in the Ipsos release

economy_bad.unit: share describing Colombia's economy as bad

observations.method: Ipsos country analysis combining direction-of-travel and issue-concern measures; the release interprets optimism as confidence in where the country is going rather than satisfaction with current conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The public release is descriptive and does not establish that political transition caused optimism or that optimism will persist; issue shares may overlap because respondents can select multiple concerns.
observations.subgroup: Adults in Colombia in the September 2026 Ipsos wave.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rising national optimism can provide political room for reform while also increasing the risk of disappointment if visible improvements do not reach employment, security, inequality, corruption, or healthcare concerns.

related_sources.claim: Ipsos historical What Worries the World archive provides monthly and long-term comparison context.
Edelman Trust Barometer provides complementary institutional and intergroup trust evidence.
OECD trust survey provides complementary evidence on policy performance, voice, and public-institution trust.

boundary: This record adds a recurring public-attention route linking healthcare, unemployment, crime, inequality, corruption, economic sentiment, political direction, and the gap between optimism and lived conditions. It uses selected highlights from a monthly Ipsos opinion survey, not administrative outcomes, causal political analysis, full country microdata, or a single globally representative estimate.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Ipsos September 2026 What Worries the World page was reviewed for survey frame, repeated-wave method, U.S. healthcare, Argentina unemployment, and Colombia direction/concern highlights and interpretation boundaries.
